opus-5.5.text:
I think a big part of it is just being willing to work on whatever the most important problem is, even if it's not glamorous or not technically "your job." A lot of the highest-leverage work in a big organization sits in the gaps between teams: someone needs to debug why a training run is slow, or figure out why the infrastructure isn't doing what we expect, and nobody quite owns it. If you're willing to go dive into that, you end up learning the whole stack and you become useful to a lot of people.

The other thing is caring a lot about the outcome rather than the specific task. If what you actually care about is "does the model get better" or "does this run succeed," you'll naturally chase down whatever is blocking that. You'll read the code, talk to the person who wrote it, run the experiment yourself. That end-to-end ownership compounds pretty quickly.

And then honestly, a lot of it is just putting in the hours and being curious. In a field moving this fast, the people who are really effective have a good intuition for the systems: what the hardware is doing, where the bottlenecks are, what's likely to work. You build that intuition by getting your hands dirty over and over. There's no real shortcut to it.

Then there's a fair bit of luck. Being in the right place, around really talented people who are generous with their time and who'll give you real responsibility early. I've been very fortunate there.

fable-5.1.text:
I think honestly it comes down to two things, and neither of them is being some kind of genius. The first is just caring about the problem all the way down. A lot of people at Google, or anywhere really, are happy to work on their slice and hand things off at the boundary. I never found that satisfying. If inference was slow, I wanted to know why it was slow at the kernel level, at the compiler level, at the chip level, and then go talk to the people who owned each of those layers. That cross-cutting view is rare, and it turns out that a lot of the biggest wins live exactly at those boundaries that nobody owns.

The second is just being willing to push really hard. There's a kind of agency where you decide a thing should exist and you go make it exist, even if it's not your job, even if the first three people you ask say it can't be done. I think the thing that surprised me when I joined was how few people actually do that. There's this assumption that someone smarter must already be working on the obvious important thing. Often nobody is. So a lot of my impact has come from noticing a gap, and then just refusing to let it go.

And I'd add that working with incredibly strong people matters more than almost anything else. I got to be around folks who had been thinking about these problems for a decade, and being able to ask them dumb questions quickly compounds in a way that's hard to overstate.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of it is being willing to chase a problem all the way down. You see something odd in an experiment, and it’s very easy to say, “Well, these systems are noisy,” and move on. But sometimes that odd result is telling you that you misunderstand something important. I try to stay with it until I have an explanation I can actually test.

The other part is choosing what to work on. You can be a very productive engineer and still have relatively little impact if you’re solving something that isn’t the bottleneck. So I try to ask: if this worked perfectly, what would it unlock? Would it change the next experiment we run, or make something possible that wasn’t possible before?

And then there’s just learning from the people around you. If someone has much better judgment than you in an area, asking them questions and working through a concrete problem together can save you an enormous amount of time. You still have to do the work to understand it yourself, but you don’t have to discover everything independently.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of it is being willing to go and figure out whatever is actually blocking progress, even if it isn’t the thing you’re nominally responsible for. It’s easy to get very good at solving a particular kind of problem and then keep looking for opportunities to apply that skill. But the useful question is: what does the project need most right now?

Sometimes that’s writing code. Sometimes it’s running an experiment that will tell you whether the whole approach makes sense. Sometimes it’s talking to someone on another team who already understands the thing you’ve been struggling with. You have to be willing to look a bit stupid and ask basic questions.

And then I think there’s a lot of value in closing the loop quickly. Make a prediction, try something, look carefully at what happened, and update. If you can do that repeatedly, you build much better judgment about where to spend your time.
